title: Going back to first principles, on purpose
excerpt: Six years shipping production agentic systems taught me how to build with LLMs. Now I'm going back through the fundamentals properly, in the open.
body:
## Why write in the open

Most of my technical growth over the last few years has come from shipping - multi-agent platforms, retrieval pipelines, fine-tuned classifiers running in production. That's real experience, but it's a specific kind: applied engineering optimises for *what works in production*, which isn't always the same muscle as understanding *why* something works from first principles.

I got properly interested in this during a university AI module that went from the fundamentals through CNNs and transformers - that's what pulled me toward this field in the first place. Since then, the applied side has moved fast, and I want to go back through the fundamentals deliberately: not because I'm starting from zero, but because the gap between "I studied this" and "I could rebuild it and explain every decision" is worth closing properly, especially with how quickly the field's moved on since.

This is the first post in a series doing exactly that - working back through the fundamentals (attention from scratch, policy gradient methods, reward modelling) and writing up what I learn, including the parts I get wrong the first time.

### What's next

- A transformer implemented from scratch, no framework shortcuts
- Notes on PPO vs DPO for preference optimisation
- Reward modelling experiments on small open datasets

If you're doing something similar - refreshing and deepening fundamentals alongside applied work - I'd like to hear what worked for you.

title: Using contextual bandits to make RAG systems adaptive
excerpt: Exploring how reinforcement learning techniques can help retrieval systems adapt as query patterns change - and the challenges that come with feedback-driven optimisation.
body:
## The problem

Static RAG configurations can degrade as query patterns change over time. Retrieval strategies that work well for one group of queries may become less effective as requirements evolve, making continuous evaluation and adaptation important.

One approach I have been exploring is using contextual bandits to help systems select between different retrieval and generation strategies based on feedback signals. By using time-weighted rewards, newer observations can have more influence than older ones when measuring performance.

### Challenges with feedback-driven optimisation

- **Reward attribution lag.** Feedback often arrives after an interaction, making it challenging to correctly associate outcomes with the actions that produced them.
- **Cold-start variance.** New strategies require exploration before enough signal exists to understand their effectiveness.
- **Reward model drift.** When evaluation relies on models such as LLM-based judges, the evaluation process itself needs monitoring to ensure optimisation targets the right behaviours.

Adaptive AI systems introduce interesting optimisation challenges and provide opportunities for building more robust retrieval pipelines.

title: Reading the scan or reading the report? A Kaggle bronze and what knee MRI models really learn
excerpt: My bronze medal in the RSNA Knee Abnormality Detection challenge, and why AI models trained on radiology reports rank the findings radiologists leave out much lower.
body: Most big medical imaging datasets aren't labelled by someone looking at every scan. That would be far too slow and expensive. Instead, the labels are pulled out of the radiology report: if the report says "ACL tear", the scan gets an ACL-tear label. That raises a question I kept coming back to during this competition: **is the AI learning what's on the scan, or what the radiologist chose to write down?** Those aren't the same thing: radiologists write for a referring doctor and often skip things they consider minor. ## The competition and the result The challenge asked for models that spot 12 abnormalities on knee MRI scans (ligament tears, meniscus tears, arthritis, fluid in the joint, synovitis, Baker's cyst, bone bruising and fracture). It was scored with AUC, a score that measures how well a model ranks the cases that have a problem above the ones that don't (1.0 is perfect; 0.5 is guessing). I finished with a **bronze medal, 506th of 6,425 teams (top 8%)**, with a private score of 0.943. On the public leaderboard I'd been 799th, so I moved up 293 places when the final scores were revealed. (Kaggle still has to verify the results, so the standings are provisional for now.) I want to be upfront about credit. The models in my medal submission weren't mine. They came from public notebooks shared by the community, mainly **goodpjw2008's** public "v27" blend recipe and reader model, with leaderboard-tuned weights from **heliosli** and work from **nartaa**, **varshithakolupuri** and **rostigor**, plus report-label sets shared by other competitors. My contributions were the expert-label weighting and the silent-findings analysis below. ## The key insight: trust the 58 expert studies The training set had about 4,400 knee MRI studies. Almost all came with only a free-text report, which competitors had to turn into labels. But **58 studies came with per-finding labels supplied by the organisers**. I call these "expert labels": a direct yes/no for each finding, rather than whatever a report happened to mention. The hidden test set's labelling method isn't published. My bet was that it's labelled more like those 58 studies than like the reports. So I took the public v27 blend and moved its per-finding weights part of the way toward whichever models ranked the expert labels best. On the private leaderboard, every expert-weighted blend I submitted scored 0.943, and every non-expert version of v27 scored 0.942. That's only +0.001, one unit at the precision Kaggle displays, so it's suggestive rather than proof. But it was the difference between being right on the bronze cutoff and sitting comfortably inside the medals. ## The silent-findings finding The 58 studies also let me test the bigger question. For each study and finding, I compared the expert label with whether the report mentioned it. That splits the expert-positive findings into two groups: - **Seen**: the expert says it's there, and the report mentions it. - **Silent**: the expert says it's there, but the report doesn't mention it. Across those 58 studies there were 193 seen findings and 47 silent ones. Then I checked how well each model ranked them against findings that were absent in both the expert label and the report. *Left: how well each model ranks reported (blue), silent (orange) and report-only (green) findings. Right: the gap between reported and silent findings. Every gap is clearly above zero. Figure from my paper; apart from my own small model, the models compared are the public notebooks credited above.* The result was consistent across every model I looked at, from the individual public models and their blends to a small model of my own: - **Reported findings** were ranked almost perfectly (AUC 0.96–0.98). - **Silent findings** were ranked much worse (AUC 0.81–0.87). - That's a **gap of about 0.10–0.16 AUC**, and for every model the 95% confidence interval excluded zero. In other words, it's very unlikely to be a fluke of which studies were in the sample. The reverse case was just as telling. When a report mentioned something the expert said *wasn't* there, models still ranked it nearly as high as a real finding (AUC 0.84–0.91). The models tend to side with the report. Synovitis (inflammation of the joint lining) was the clearest example. Over half its expert-positive cases (14 of 27) weren't mentioned in the report, and most models ranked those unreported cases noticeably lower. I also ruled out boring explanations. Swapping left and right knee predictions made every model worse, so it isn't a left/right mix-up. Misranking also wasn't linked to how many MRI series a study had, so the models weren't simply picking the wrong series. Could better blending fix it? Only a little. Re-weighting the blend toward the expert labels narrowed the gap from 0.122 to 0.112. ## Why this matters for medical AI Test a report-trained model against more report-derived labels and this gap is invisible, because you're checking it against the habits it learned from. During the competition, a holdout set scored with report labels actually favoured a change that the expert labels, and later the leaderboard, rejected. My takeaway: even a small set of image-level expert labels is worth having, and results should be reported separately for findings the report left out. One overall AUC can hide a real drop on exactly the cases a radiologist didn't flag. ## Limitations This is a small study. There are only 58 studies and 47 silent findings, nearly a third of them synovitis, so the exact size of the gap is uncertain, even though its direction is consistent. The labels for whether each report mentioned a finding were made by an AI assistant under my direction, and neither a clinician nor I checked them by hand. We also don't know how the organisers produced the expert labels, so they aren't guaranteed to be ground truth. Out of respect for the RSNA data licence, the paper and this post use aggregate statistics only. No images, report text or per-study labels. ## Read more **Read the full paper on arXiv: [ARXIV_LINK_PLACEHOLDER]** You can also find me on Kaggle: [codecraftedbydan](https://www.kaggle.com/codecraftedbydan). A note on tools: I used AI assistants to help write the analysis code, produce the figures and draft this post. The research question, the expert-label weighting, the decisions and the conclusions are my own. Thanks to RSNA and Kaggle for running the challenge, and to everyone who shared public notebooks. This result was built on their work.
